strengths: Introduces MMEarth-Bench, a useful new multimodal Earth-observation benchmark with five global tasks, 12 aligned modalities, and both random and geographic (Africa-held-out) test splits, directly addressing gaps in prior EO benchmarks.

Provides a broad empirical study: seven pretrained models with diverse architectures and input modalities, evaluated under finetuning and linear probing, low-shot subsets, random vs. geographic splits, three random seeds, and statistical tests.

TTT-MMR is simple, model-agnostic, and consistently improves over the joint-training baseline across models, tasks, and both test splits; geographic batching offers a sensible regularization/specialization trade-off.
The supplement is unusually thorough, with data generation details, modality statistics, raw results, compute times, visualization tooling, and reproducibility information.
weaknesses: The TTT contribution is under-ablated: there is no comparison to single-modality or subset-modality TTT, no analysis isolating the effect of per-modality gradient normalization, and no comparison to existing test-time adaptation methods (e.g., TENT-style, TTT-MAE, entropy-based variants), so it is unclear how much of the gain comes from multimodal reconstruction versus generic test-time self-supervision.

The species task raises benchmark-validity concerns: labels are derived from IUCN range polygons rather than observed occurrences, and models that receive geolocation input (Copernicus-FM) achieve near-perfect random-split mAP, suggesting location/ecoregion leakage and possibly an overly easy or confounded task.

Model comparisons are not fully controlled because different models receive different input modalities (RGB, S2, S1, DEM, geolocation, date), so rankings may reflect available inputs rather than representation quality alone.

The geographic generalization claim is based only on holding out Africa; while relevant, this limits broader conclusions about global geographic generalization, and some tasks show weak or inconsistent geographic gains.
TTT-MMR is computationally expensive at inference time (roughly 0.9 s/sample for some models versus 0.007 s for a standard forward pass), which may limit large-scale practical deployment.

Some reported regression scores are highly negative (especially soil OC and soil N in the geographic split), and several TTT improvements are small in absolute terms; practical significance beyond statistical significance is not always clear.

strengths: Introduces MMEARTH-BENCH, a substantial new global multimodal benchmark with five environmental tasks, 12 aligned modalities, random and geographic test splits, and low-shot training subsets, which is a useful resource for evaluating geospatial foundation models.

Provides a broad benchmark of seven pretrained models across multiple data regimes, with multiple seeds, finetuning and linear-probing results, and extensive supplementary details on dataset construction.

Proposes TTT-MMR, a simple model-agnostic test-time adaptation method that uses multimodal reconstruction losses and shows consistent improvements over the joint-training baseline across models, tasks, and both random and geographic splits.
Includes statistical significance testing for TTT improvements and reports practical inference costs and visualization tooling, supporting reproducibility and usability.

Highlights an important and underexplored problem: geographic generalization in multimodal Earth observation, with empirical evidence that many pretrained models still generalize poorly to held-out regions.
The dataset construction is documented in considerable detail in the supplementary material, including sampling, modality extraction, and split generation.
weaknesses: The species task is potentially invalid as an environmental representation benchmark: labels are derived from IUCN range polygons rather than actual occurrence observations, and geolocation is included as a modality. Because tiles are sampled inside/outside range polygons, models may largely memorize spatial range geometry rather than learn transferable environmental features. No ablation without geolocation or against non-spatial baselines is provided, and the near-perfect random-split mAP of some models suggests possible task triviality or label leakage.

The biomass task uses sparse GEDI L4A footprint measurements as pixel-level labels, but the manuscript does not specify how missing labels are masked during training or evaluation, how many labeled pixels exist per tile, or how sparse supervision affects the reported R2. This makes the biomass results difficult to interpret and reproduce.

Missing modalities are pervasive and not adequately handled: Sentinel-1 is missing in roughly 60–86% of tiles for most tasks, and other modalities have missing values. The paper claims 12 modalities per tile but does not describe a consistent missing-modality strategy during joint training or benchmarking, which may compromise fair comparisons across models.

Potential pretraining leakage is not ruled out. The benchmark uses the same modalities and data sources as the MMEarth pretraining dataset, and MPMAE was pretrained on MMEarth. No spatial overlap analysis between pretraining and benchmark tiles is provided, so reported MPMAE performance may be inflated.

The methodological contribution is incremental: TTT with reconstruction is already known, and the paper only compares against a joint-training baseline, not against other test-time adaptation or self-supervised TTT signals. There are no ablations on the number/type of reconstruction modalities, gradient normalization, batching strategy, learning rate, or number of iterations.

Reported TTT gains are often small in absolute terms. On several tasks, geographic-split R2 remains negative or near zero after adaptation, and some improvements over joint training merely recover performance lost relative to standard finetuning. The practical significance of the method is therefore unclear.

No non-deep baselines, such as random forests or geolocation/climate-only regressors, are evaluated for the soil, biomass, or species tasks. Without such baselines, it is hard to assess whether the pretrained models add meaningful value beyond simple spatial or environmental covariates.

The geographic test split is a single held-out continent (Africa), and for some soil tasks the geographic test set contains only a few hundred tiles. This limits the robustness of conclusions about global geographic generalization.

The paper lacks critical discussion of limitations and failure modes, including computational overhead (up to ~0.91 s/sample, over 100x a standard forward pass), privacy/licensing constraints for some datasets, and the unresolved validity concerns for species and biomass evaluation.

strengths: The paper makes a strong datasets/benchmarks contribution: MMEarth-Bench provides five global environmental tasks with 12 aligned modalities, low-shot subsets, and both random and geographic test splits, filling a real gap in multimodal EO benchmarking.

The benchmark design is thoughtful: all tasks share the same 12 modalities, include pixel- and tile-level data, cover regression and multi-label classification, and explicitly evaluate geographic generalization with a held-out Africa split.

The empirical study is broad and well documented: seven pretrained models with diverse architectures and input modalities are benchmarked with three seeds, error bars, finetuning and linear probing, and extensive supplementary raw results and implementation details.

The proposed TTT-MMR and TTT-MMR-GEO are model-agnostic, can use modalities not accepted by the pretrained encoder, and improve over the joint-training baseline across models, tasks, and splits according to the reported rankings and significance tests.

The paper yields useful scientific findings: multimodal pretraining generally helps, but geographic generalization remains weak; additionally, multimodal finetuning can sometimes hurt out-of-distribution performance, which is a nuanced and valuable observation for the EO community.

Reproducibility is generally strong: detailed data generation, split construction, normalization statistics, hyperparameters, metrics, compute costs, code, and visualization tools are provided, and the work builds on public datasets and pretrained models.
weaknesses: The method contribution is under-validated against existing test-time adaptation baselines. The comparisons are mainly joint training versus TTT-MMR variants, with no TENT, input-reconstruction TTT, single-modality TTT, or other TTA/TTT baselines, so the specific benefit of multimodal reconstruction is not isolated.

There are no clear ablations for key design choices such as per-modality gradient normalization, the number of reconstruction modalities, or random versus geographic batching beyond the main two variants. This limits understanding of why TTT-MMR works and when it should be preferred.

Geographic generalization is evaluated with only one held-out region (Africa). While well motivated, this is insufficient to support broad claims about global generalization; multiple leave-region-out splits or additional held-out continents would make the benchmark stronger.

Missing modality patterns may confound the geographic split results. Sentinel-1 is missing for a large fraction of tiles, and modality availability likely varies by region; without controlling for this, some geographic performance drops may reflect missing inputs rather than domain shift alone.

Some tasks have possible shortcut or leakage concerns: geolocation, biome, and ecoregion are provided as inputs, while species labels are derived from IUCN range polygons. This may make it easier to memorize geographic ranges rather than learn transferable environmental representations.

The TTT inference cost is high, roughly two orders of magnitude slower than a standard forward pass in some cases. Although the paper reports <1 sec/sample, global-scale deployment trade-offs and latency/energy implications are not discussed deeply enough.

License and redistribution restrictions for some datasets, especially soil tasks (CC BY-NC) and species data (Terms of Use), may limit open benchmark adoption and long-term reproducibility despite the project page and code release.

The main results are sometimes summarized by ranks and significance tests while effect sizes can be small or near zero, especially for some geographic species results. The claim of improvement across all models, tasks, and splits would be more convincing with clearer effect-size analysis in the main paper.
The benchmark is deliberately single-timestamp, which excludes temporal modeling. This is acknowledged, but it limits applicability to many important EO tasks where time series are central.

The method assumes all task modalities are available at test time, either directly or via coordinate-based extraction. In many operational settings, this may not hold, and the paper does not fully analyze performance under realistic missing-modality or partially available-modality scenarios.

strengths: Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, this is best viewed as a benchmark/dataset contribution with an accompanying method; I assess it primarily on those terms. MMEarth-Bench fills a real gap by providing 12 aligned EO modalities, five environmental tasks, globally distributed data, low-shot subsets, and both random and geographic (Africa) test splits, with detailed documentation of data generation and licensing.

The benchmark is comprehensive and useful: 8 pretrained geospatial models (RGB-only, S2-only, multimodal) are evaluated under low-shot and geographic generalization settings, with extensive raw results, rankings, statistical tests, and long-tail analyses. The dataset/code/visualization tool release and detailed appendix support reproducibility.

The proposed TTT-MMR is simple and model-agnostic: it repurposes all test-time task modalities as reconstruction targets, normalizes gradients per modality, and adapts the encoder without test labels. The geographic batching variant (TTT-MMR-GEO) is a sensible addition and shows especially convincing gains on long-tail samples.

The experimental analysis is thorough: modality importance, iteration counts, linear probing, reconstruction quality, compute time, per-model rankings, and multiple random seeds are reported. Claims about gains over joint training are generally well supported and statistically tested.
The paper is clearly written and well organized, with a detailed appendix, dataset explorer, and transparent reporting of limitations of existing benchmarks.
weaknesses: For a method paper, the evaluation lacks comparison to existing TTA/TTT methods (e.g., TENT, READ, rotation/masked-reconstruction TTT, or pseudo-label adaptation) on this benchmark. Demonstrating improvement over joint training alone does not establish that TTT-MMR is better than prior test-time adaptation approaches.

The species occurrence task uses IUCN range polygons as labels, which are expert range maps rather than actual occurrence records. This likely inflates performance and limits the task's validity as a true species occurrence benchmark, even if multi-label range prediction is still a meaningful task.

Geographic generalization is evaluated with only a single held-out region (Africa). This is a relevant but coarse split and may conflate geographic domain shift with label distribution shift; robustness to multiple held-out continents or other underrepresented regions is not tested.

TTT-MMR requires auxiliary task modalities at test time and a jointly trained modality decoder. Practical deployments may not have all modalities available or aligned, and the method's robustness to missing, noisy, or misaligned modalities is not extensively explored beyond excluding missing modalities.

The paper reports that a randomly initialized multimodal model is competitive with pretrained models given enough labels. This candid finding raises questions about the difficulty of the benchmark and how much practical value the pretraining/adaptation pipeline adds; further disentangling pretraining gains from labeled data gains would strengthen the paper.

There is no dedicated limitations or broader societal-impact discussion. For an environmental benchmark, discussing potential misuse of species range predictions and label uncertainty would improve the submission.

strengths: The paper introduces MMEarth-Bench, a multimodal Earth-observation benchmark with five globally distributed tasks, 12 aligned modalities shared across tasks, low-data subsets, and both random and geographic test splits, which addresses a real gap in evaluating multimodal geospatial models.

The empirical study is extensive: eight pretrained models are benchmarked across multiple architectures and modality settings, with finetuning and linear probing, low-shot regimes, geographic generalization, and long-tail analysis; the appendix provides substantial implementation and reproducibility details.

The proposed TTT-MMR is simple and model-agnostic: it uses all available test-time modalities as reconstruction targets with per-modality gradient normalization, requiring only a lightweight modality decoder and no architecture-specific batch-norm/FiLM modifications.

The paper shows that TTT-MMR can improve average model rankings and long-tail performance, and it documents data sources, licenses, code, and an interactive explorer, supporting reproducibility and reuse.
weaknesses: The method is evaluated only against joint training and not against standard TTA/TTT baselines (e.g., TENT, TTT with rotation prediction, masked reconstruction, or pseudo-label adaptation), so the claimed advantage of TTT-MMR over existing test-time adaptation methods is not established.

The abstract and contributions overclaim that TTT-MMR improves performance 'across all models and tasks on both test splits,' but the appendix and raw results contain negative or non-significant improvements (e.g., soil OC, Galileo, ConvNeXtV2A-MM), making the main claim inconsistent with the evidence.

The geographic generalization evaluation relies on a single held-out continent (Africa) and is confounded with substantial label-distribution shift; multiple held-out regions and better-controlled splits are needed to support broad 'global' adaptation claims. Random tile splits may also suffer from spatial autocorrelation and overstate performance.

The methodological novelty is incremental: test-time training with auxiliary reconstruction/SSL losses is already established, and the added multimodal reconstruction loss and geographic batching are largely heuristic and not deeply ablated against relevant alternatives.

The TTT inference cost is very high relative to a standard forward pass (~0.9 s/sample vs ~0.007 s/sample, roughly two orders of magnitude slower), which limits practical deployment at global scales, yet efficiency, accuracy trade-offs, and energy cost are not discussed in depth.

The benchmark's most striking result—a randomly initialized multimodal model being competitive with pretrained models given enough labels—is not fully unpacked; it raises concerns about whether the benchmark effectively measures the benefits of large-scale pretraining, which is central to the paper's motivation.

The species task is built from IUCN range polygons rather than observed occurrence records, and the nearly saturated random-split mAP (e.g., 0.99) suggests possible spatial autocorrelation or label leakage; this task may not robustly test multimodal reasoning.

The analysis of failure cases is limited: negative transfer in soil organic carbon and some geographic splits is not explained, modality importance is tested with only one seed in a leave-one-out setting, and the validation-based iteration selection may not adapt well to the held-out target domain.

strengths: Introduces MMEarth-Bench, a valuable multimodal Earth observation benchmark with five environmental tasks, 12 aligned modalities, global data, random and geographic test splits, and low-data regimes (100%, 50%, 5%), filling an important gap for evaluating geospatial foundation models under limited labels and domain shift.

Provides extensive benchmarking of eight pretrained models plus from-scratch baselines, revealing important empirical findings: geographic generalization remains poor, multimodal pretraining helps in low-shot settings, and a randomly initialized multimodal model can be competitive with sufficient labels.

Proposes TTT-MMR, a model-agnostic test-time training method that uses all available modalities as reconstruction targets, with per-modality gradient normalization; it requires no architecture-specific modifications and is applicable to regression and classification tasks.
Introduces TTT-MMR-GEO with geographic batching, showing a useful trade-off between regularization and specialization and improved long-tail/rare-sample performance, especially for regression tasks.

Experimental validation is thorough: multiple seeds, statistical significance testing, modality-importance analysis, iteration-count analysis, compute-time reporting, and raw results in the appendix. The dataset construction and preprocessing pipeline are documented in detail, supporting reproducibility.

The paper is clearly written and well organized, with informative figures and tables. It provides strong connections to related work in geospatial pretraining, domain adaptation, and test-time adaptation.
The benchmark and method have practical relevance to the computer vision and remote sensing communities, and the released dataset, code, and visualization tool support future research.
weaknesses: The claim that TTT-MMR improves performance across all models, tasks, and splits is somewhat overstated: per-model relative-improvement results show negative or negligible changes for some models on the random split (e.g., Galileo and ConvNeXtV2A-MM), and some gains are modest in absolute terms.

The method assumes that all 12 task modalities are available at test time and can be used as reconstruction targets. This may not hold in many real-world downstream deployments, where only a subset of modalities is available; missing-modality behavior is handled simply by exclusion and is not extensively evaluated.

The paper lacks head-to-head comparisons with existing test-time adaptation methods such as TENT or other multimodal TTA approaches, although the authors argue that TENT is not suitable for regression and READ assumes different modality encoding. Additional comparisons, where feasible, would strengthen the empirical case.

The geographic generalization evaluation uses only Africa as the held-out region. This is a meaningful but narrow test of geographic shift; broader held-out continents or multiple geographic splits would better support claims of global generalization.

Some benchmark labels are derived from modeled or aggregated products (e.g., IUCN range polygons for species occurrence, GEDI samples for biomass, and WoSIS soil data). These may contain noise, sampling bias, and spatial autocorrelation that affect the interpretation of the results, even if the paper acknowledges data sources and limitations.

The practical significance of TTT-MMR gains is sometimes limited: several geographic-split results still have low or negative R^2 on soil organic carbon and soil nitrogen, and the reported improvements are often small in absolute metric terms.

The paper does not include an explicit limitations section for its own benchmark and method, although limitations of prior benchmarks are discussed. A focused discussion of limitations and potential negative societal impacts would improve transparency.
